item.title: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
item.description: A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels. Read more Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet? The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency. Advertisement But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia. Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels” , but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates. Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change. Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”. Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance

item.title: F1 in Las Vegas: You've never seen an F1 race like this before
item.description: Las Vegas welcomed Formula 1 to its streets this past weekend. And for the first time since the event’s inception in 2023 , the Grand Prix delivered on a long-promised spectacle. The racing was closer to an IndyCar oval race than anything F1 fans will have seen since slipstreaming was the order of the day at places like Monza and Hockenheim, back when humans were still landing on the Moon and downforce had yet to fundamentally change racing. The Vegas street circuit—the one that looks like an upside-down pig—is an extreme outlier on the calendar. It has plenty of long straights, so this year’s cars still suffer from energy starvation throughout the lap, as the inadequate size of their lithium-ion hybrid batteries means they become depleted very quickly , leaving the cars on just over half power with their V6 engines operating without the benefit of the hybrid’s electric motor. But the 17 turns are mostly all low speed, so there’s no risk of seeing the cars driving demoralizingly slowly through corners that are supposed to test one’s mettle . Read full article Comments

item.title: Trump says he won't allow US companies to build datacenters abroad
item.description: US President Donald Trump has threatened a "tremendous tax" on American companies building datacenters overseas, arguing that the infrastructure should stay at home to preserve the country's AI lead over China. Speaking at a White House press conference after returning from the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Trump portrayed AI leadership as a contest America could not afford to lose. Trump went on to say that "we're not going to allow our companies to build datacenters outside of our country," adding that "they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else and it was very destructive to our country." The threat appeared to catch even his own administration unbriefed. "I haven't even said that to my people, but I'm telling them now," Trump said. The Official White House Rapid Response account posted a video clip on X. We asked the White House if the president intends to follow through, and we will let you know if we get an answer. Trump said: "We're not going to allow companies to build datacenters in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them. We want them to do it here." The threat comes amid concerns that Chinese entities were able to use Nvidia's cutting-edge GPUs for training AI models by accessing cloud services hosted in third countries. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued new rules to try and crack down on this practice last week. "We're not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, as China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump repeated. "We're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it. They want to build that one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen," he added. Google is expanding its facilities in Finland, including one recently in the news because the developer had reportedly illegally felled 250,000 trees to make way for it. Such a policy seems unlikely to be allowed by Congress, where both houses will be under the control of the Democrats when the new term begins in January. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft already operate global datacenter networks to serve customers in different regions. Restrictions on further overseas construction would complicate those businesses. Omdia chief analyst Roy Illsley expressed doubt that this is a serious threat. "There will be ways around that if he does impose some executive order, and the ability to build datacenters is not just an American skill, many countries can build them, it is the equipment in them that is mostly US," he told The Register . "So I do not take this seriously as it would not work, there is no such thing as a US datacenter, they are made up of thousands of components from all over the globe. He could stop US capital from being invested in those countries, but that could have trade consequences." Mike Kharchenko of European hosting firm HostZealot said there are good reasons why the c

item.title: New Outlook's attachment issues sent users into the arms of its predecessor
item.description: A recent update broke attachment handling for some New Outlook users, prompting Microsoft to recommend switching to the web or Classic version of its email client. Things are going swimmingly for New Outlook, the email client that Microsoft would very much like users to migrate to. A code change meant that for some users, opening or uploading email attachments failed. It took the company two attempts to fix the problem. Microsoft confirmed there were issues on November 20, as reports that customers were having problems with attachments began rolling in. By the end of the day, the company had added inline images in email to the litany of woe and "paused the rollout of a recent client update that may be contributing to attachment failures." The advice for affected users was to switch to the web version, or use Outlook Classic to open or upload attachments and view inline images. The good news was that Microsoft produced a fix. The bad news was that this fix only resolved problems with Office attachments and inline images, leaving other attachment types affected, according to incident notice EX1561765. The Windows behemoth tried again with a "supplemental fix" and reported the remaining problems resolved on November 21. Users needed to close and reopen New Outlook for the fix to take effect. Microsoft said it had tested the fixes before deployment. Administrators might reasonably wish the original update had received the same attention. The preliminary root cause was a "recent update to the code which supports embedded web content unexpectedly caused impact." The clock is ticking for Outlook Classic. Microsoft is clear that New Outlook is the future, though Classic Outlook will remain available until at least 2029. The fact that the company had to suggest that affected users fall back on the old warhorse to perform that rarely used email activity – attachment handling – is less than confidence-inspiring. Still, by the time Outlook Classic is finally put out to pasture, we're sure Microsoft's habit of sending out broken updates will also be a thing of the past. Right? ®

item.title: Norway links energy firm cyberattacks to critical Azure API Management flaw
item.description: Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations. According to a nonpublic advisory, seen by The Register , Microsoft said the attacks, which have already affected two major energy companies , only impact customers on Azure API Management Classic tiers, not Azure API Management v2. It said of the now-patched vuln: "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue." Microsoft linked exposure to Classic-tier configurations that did not follow its network security guidance or stored secrets directly in APIM rather than referencing them from Azure Key Vault. Microsoft directs customers to its security guidance for the recommended configuration. The advisory lists potentially exposed secrets, including named values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs. Security expert Anders Kristiansen warned that stolen credentials could also give attackers access to services behind APIM. "If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects, outside APIM," he wrote . "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid." Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) urged organizations using APIM to assume their secrets and named values had been exposed and rotate all tokens and secrets. The agency also advised mapping the information accessible through each APIM instance to assess the potential scope of any compromise. NSM credited Norway's energy sector with first detecting the vulnerability last week. It named gas giant Equinor and hydropower company Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations. The authority commended Equinor for its early detection and rapid information-sharing, and warned that growing use of AI increased the risk of further exploitation. "The vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and also beyond Norway's borders," it said . "NSM has close dialogue and cooperation with national and international partners and businesses about the situation. "When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors will be able to attempt to exploit it. Rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence is affecting the situation. This poses a risk to Norwegian businesses." Customers who spoke to The Register warned that forgotten development and test instances could leave more organizations exposed. The extent of exploitation remains unclear. Microsoft said it identified the security issue on November 18 and automatically applied a mitigation to close the access path the following day. The Windows giant said customers still needed to investigate wh

item.title: Cleverbridge admits attackers stole customers' credit card and CVV numbers. Yep, you read that right
item.description: Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization. The Germany-headquartered company, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4. In an incident update , Cleverbridge said it had cut off the intruders' access and launched an investigation that later established payment card information had been copied from its systems. The public notice doesn't spell out exactly what was stolen, but an email sent to affected customers, seen by The Register , fills in some rather important blanks. "Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details," the company told customers. Email addresses, billing addresses, and phone numbers were also among the information potentially exposed, although Cleverbridge reckons account passwords escaped the breach. More concerning are the stolen CVV codes. PCI DSS rules prohibit retaining card verification codes after authorization, even in encrypted form. Cleverbridge hasn't explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether the criminals intercepted them during payment processing. The company didn't respond to The Register's questions about the breach. Cleverbridge handles the business of selling software online, from taking payments to managing subscriptions, and its client roster includes some familiar names in enterprise IT, such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, and Plesk. That doesn't mean customers of all those companies had their card details stolen. Cleverbridge hasn't named the vendors affected by the intrusion, nor has it disclosed how many people were caught up in the breach or how long the hackers were poking around its systems. In its notification to customers, the company said it had contacted data protection authorities, payment card schemes, and its payment partners, and was working with a specialist police cybercrime unit. It began notifying affected individuals on November 20, more than two weeks after discovering the intrusion. Affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance. That may help detect identity misuse, but it won't stop a crook armed with their card number, expiration date, and CVV from attempting a fraudulent purchase. Two years of credit monitoring is a nice gesture, but customers whose card numbers and CVVs are now in criminal hands might prefer a new bit of plastic. ®

item.title: Capita CEO leaves following pensions contract disaster
item.description: Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez has stepped down with immediate effect as the outsourcer warned of sharply lower profits next year, nearly a year after its troubled takeover of administration of the UK's Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS). In a statement , Capita said CFO Pablo Andres had become CEO, with group financial controller Gemma Bate-Williams succeeding him as finance chief. Capita now expects adjusted operating profit for 2027 to be £85 million to £95 million below previous expectations. That includes £15 million to £25 million in additional costs under a pensions recovery plan agreed with the Cabinet Office, alongside pressure from contract exits and other trading headwinds. Shares fell around 70 percent following the announcement. The company – which is also coming under fire for its £370 million contract with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) – said it had made significant progress in its transformation and strategic simplification. It also plans to raise around £190 million through a share issue in the first half of 2027 to reduce borrowing and to "allow the business to move forward from a more stable foundation," subject to support from its financial creditors. James Preece, principal analyst at UK tech research firm Megabuyte, said: "Slow motion car crash comes to mind. It has been a turnaround job for coming up to four years now, with long-suffering shareholders watching dozens of disposals and business exits fail to arrest a structural decline in both margins and growth. "Today's update suggests that management's underlying forecast assumptions alongside other more transient factors were still too punchy, and the leverage situation now calls for action. The share price reaction suggests confidence in this being a one-and-done raise is limited," he said. Capita took over administration of the scheme in December 2025 under a seven-year, £239 million contract, after which The Register exclusively revealed problems with its online systems . The vendor promised AI and automation, but the takeover brought a glitchy online portal, while some members struggled to receive pension payments. By January, it was clear the service was seriously failing, leaving some retired civil servants struggling to make ends meet. Capita missed its deadline to restore normal service by the end of June. It subsequently told MPs that all but the most complex cases would return to normal service by September. The pensions scheme serves around 1.7 million members. Media reports and MPs have described members feeling upset, frustrated, and ignored, with some waiting months for payments. The government said it had withheld £10 million in payments over Capita's performance during the transition of the pensions service and was negotiating further penalties. It also appointed an auditor to assess the case for further penalties for Capita's performance on the contract. Last month, the National Audit Office launched an investigation into the CSPS contract. item.title: Old-school Linux desktops find fresh routes to Wayland
item.description: Xfce's next release is taking shape for 2027, while MATE users have fresh options for moving their familiar desktop onto Wayland. One of the oldest surviving Linux desktops has a relatively slow release schedule: new stable releases of Xfce tend to appear every two years. The project just updated its release engineering roadmap for the forthcoming Xfce 4.22, and it looks like the next version won't arrive until early next year. We covered the release of Xfce 4.20 in December 2024, but 4.22 is still incubating. The roadmap schedules its first prerelease and feature freeze for December 15, 2026, followed by a second prerelease on January 15, 2027. A third prerelease is optional, and neither that nor the final release has a date. February or March might be plausible, but that's our guess, not the project's promise. The Xfce developers tend not to rush into things. Wayland development continues in 4.22, building on the preliminary support in 4.20. The team is also working on its own compositor, xfwl4, although the roadmap doesn't promise feature parity with X11. (In Wayland terminology, the "compositor" is the combined display server and window manager.) The compositor has its own development roadmap . The name is a nod to the current Xfce X11 window manager, which is called xfwm4 . The main developer of the new xfwl4 compositor is Brian Tarricone , who has been working on other parts of Xfce since 2004. Back in July, he shared a blog post about his use of generative-AI coding assistants called LLMs and xfwl4 . He says: "So yes, I use Claude quite a bit while developing xfwl4. I don't vibe-code, ever, and I probably use the LLM to generate less code than most people do. After all, building things with code is my hobby and passion (and I'm lucky I got to do it professionally for a quarter century), and driving an LLM is kinda boring." We find this somewhat reassuring, but any really passionate anti-LLM Xfce users reading this may be glad that the release schedules of Ubuntu LTS versions and Xfce stable releases are so far out of sync – sticking with Xubuntu 26.04 means there's no immediate need to adopt the new LLM-assisted compositor. Or, of course, simply keep using X11 instead of Wayland – although that might eventually mean choosing a distro that maintains X11 support, perhaps through XLibre, which has other drawbacks for some. There are other options, too. We've also seen an independent fork of xfwm4 called xfwm4-gl . It's in active development and uses OpenGL to perform window compositing directly, while the current version uses the now rather old Xrender extension . Labwc and MATE Wayland, and Wayfire, and Polo too Last year, when we looked at the release candidate of openSUSE Leap 16.0 , we found that it ran Xfce on Wayland by replacing Xfwm4 with the labwc compositor that we first saw in PiOS 5.2 . This worked well – about the only difference we could find was the absence of some window-management shortcuts. (Saying that, this vulture is stil

item.title: Airbus may be leaving Microsoft Office, but for its 36,000 defense staff, Office isn't leaving them
item.description: Airbus has a plan to phase out Microsoft Office, but about 22 percent of its roughly 165,000 employees will stay on it because their sensitive data must remain on-premise. In March 2018, Airbus signed a contract with Google to move its workforce - 130,000 strong at that time - onto the cloud-based Workspace suite. Years later, compatibility issues mean some users still need Excel. Catherine Jestin, Airbus's executive vice president of digital, told The Register that Google is still working to resolve software interface conflicts between departments and improve features. Last year, for example, Google tripled the number of cells available in Sheets, which let Airbus "reduce significantly the number of users on Microsoft." This year, Google improved the compatibility of document watermarking. Contracts, for instance, are often exported from Excel to Sheets by one department, edited by another, and sent back. "Sometimes we had compatibility issues when you were commenting, the comments were lost, or they were not transferable in one way or the other," she said. "Now they [Google] have made it totally compatible, which means that it makes it much easier for us to decommission people working on contracts… the legal department, the sales department, purchasing department, making it much easier to have that internal collaboration." Airbus and Google have a roadmap to eliminate Microsoft Office. Jestin expects the migration to finish in "another two to three years." Not every part of the company will switch. The Defence division , which accounts for the 22 percent (more than 36,000 people), will keep using classic Microsoft Office. "We will not get 100 percent out of Microsoft because again, for the defense industry people, they cannot [use] Microsoft Office 365 or Google Workspace, they have to stay on-premise, and the only solution that is available on-premise is Microsoft. So Microsoft Office will remain for colleagues who are working in the defense and space programs." As we pointed out a year ago, kicking the Microsoft habit is no easy feat. ®

item.title: Solape Fayemi Launches Saina Properties Across Four Markets
item.description: For many people, buying property is one of the biggest financial decisions they will ever make. Yet, knowing who to trust, how to verify ownership and whether a property is worth the investment can make the process overwhelming. It is a challenge Solape Fayemi hopes to address with the launch of Saina Properties , a real estate company now operating across Nigeria, the United Kingdom, the United States and the United Arab Emirates. Officially unveiled at an event held on 17 November at the Marriott Hotel, Ikeja GRA, Lagos, Saina Properties is built around a simple idea: property ownership should be guided by sound advice, proper verification and professional support, not just the excitement of closing a deal. For Solape, whose experience in the investment industry shaped her understanding of money, risk and wealth creation, the decision to establish the company came from recognising the need for a more considered approach to real estate. “We are not building Saina Properties because the world needs another company selling properties. We are building Saina because we believe there is room for a different kind of real estate experience. One where advice comes before the transaction, where due diligence is not treated as an inconvenience, and where people are encouraged to ask questions, understand their options and make informed decisions,” she said at the launch. That philosophy is reflected in the company’s three core areas of expertise: Advisory & Verification, Sales & Brokerage, and Developments . Rather than focusing solely on connecting buyers to properties, Saina brings together the guidance investors need to assess opportunities, the support required to navigate property transactions, and involvement in real estate development. The company is also building on experience gained before its official launch, having supported more than 25 clients with property opportunities across different markets. An important part of its proposition is the role of professional expertise in protecting property investors. Fayemi’s position raises a familiar question: people consult doctors for medical concerns and lawyers for legal matters, so why do some investors leave significant property decisions in the hands of relatives simply because they are available or familiar with the location? While trust and family relationships matter, they do not automatically translate into the technical knowledge needed to assess a property, verify its documentation or understand its investment potential. These decisions require proper checks, market understanding and accountability. With its operations spanning four markets, Saina Properties aims to support individuals and investors looking to navigate property ownership with greater clarity, whether they are buying, selling or exploring development opportunities. Its guiding promise captures the thinking behind the business: “ With Saina Properties, you own with certainty.” Solape Fayemi is the Chief Executive Officer of Sa

item.title: When Microsoft, Apple, and the FAA can't keep it up, it's a system of a down
item.description: No Access November is going well this year. Among the many organizations to adopt Outage As A Service (OAAS) were Microsoft , Apple , the FAA , and any number of European supermarkets . Even the NSA has succumbed. For us, at least, outage is word of the year. It's certainly deeply embedded in the public mind, with schoolchildren reportedly referring to the 19th century Irish famine as "the potato outage." There's no danger of an outrage outage. OAAS is synonymous with infrastructure failure, a more useful term that begins to hint at cause and cure as well as effect. In all of the latest crop, what we know is depressingly familiar. Microsoft's O365 meltdown was a cascading failure caused by a botched upgrade that took stuff offline and melted down as it tried to come back. The FAA was a migration from Jurassic hardware that wasn't end of life so much as living fossil. The Eurofridge-cum-fondue-maker was a control system so badly written it fell apart if you raised an eyebrow at it. Clearly, nobody had. Until now. These are all different classes of OAAS that have been around for decades. Security-based outages are still outages, and a packet flood is still a packet flood whether it's a botnet DDoS or finger trouble in the config dashboard. Each of them has a root cause with obvious fixes – a faulty mental model of network/server interaction, chronic underfunding, a complete supply chain with little cyber-security expertise. All these, like the poor, will be with us always. They won't fix themselves. Infrastructure that works is invisible, and invisible things are forgotten until they break. What's needed is an infrastructure that watches itself, that is designed to be adaptive and resilient, one that refuses to connect to danger and nulls out any that gets through. There have been attempts to create a ground-up architecture that is inherently risk resistant. One such is SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation On Next-generation networks). It redesigns routing between domains around explicit path selection, separate control and data planes, and mechanisms for trust and failure isolation. The result is a very resilient, very reliable, and very secure infrastructure that reflects the designers' tenet that you can't patch the internet into any of these things. Start from scratch or GTFO. SCION started about 15 years ago, and it works well enough to be adopted by entities like the Secure Swiss Finance Network . If the Gnomes of Zurich trust it, no higher accreditation exists. Well, it was designed by ETH Zürich. Where you won't find it is almost everywhere else. The internet is like Switzerland in the same way the Amazon rainforest is like Central Park. There are trees and sometimes it rains. It is unwise to infer anything else. Given you can't manicure existing infrastructure into true resilience, the only other option is evolution. A couple of billion years of continued life on Earth has proved this is the only way to re-engineer complex systems wh

item.title: How Mary Akinwola Graduated with a Distinction from Oxford After Receiving Multiple Scholarships
item.description: Mary Akinwola graduated from the University of Oxford after receiving the Chevening and Mastercard Foundation Scholarships. My name is Mary Akinwola. I’m a physiotherapist, a strategy consultant, a healthcare entrepreneur, and I recently graduated from the University of Oxford with a distinction in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation. I have probably said that last part a hundred times since getting my results, and honestly, I don’t think I’m tired of saying it yet. Haha! One thing about me is that I like to be involved. I am sometimes curious about things that have absolutely nothing to do with what I’m supposed to be doing, and I genuinely enjoy working with people. I like organising things, bringing people together, and seeing an idea move forward to get accomplished. So I have known that going to Oxford was never going to be just about getting a master’s degree. Let me explain how I ended up there. I studied Physiotherapy at the University of Ibadan, where I graduated with First-Class Honours. During my undergraduate years, I was involved in quite a lot outside academics: student leadership, journalism, research, community health programmes and advocacy. My involvement in community health exposed me to how differently people experience healthcare depending on where they live, what they can afford and what information they have access to. I loved being a physiotherapist, and that allowed me to interrogate questions that went beyond individual patient care. Why do some people receive good healthcare while others struggle to access even basic services? How do we make healthcare more affordable? What role can technology play? And why do some seemingly good healthcare programmes struggle to produce lasting change? Eventually, I realised I wanted to study and work in a field that constantly seeks to improve health systems. I researched different programmes across the US and UK, hoping to study at institutions that have international audiences where I could build a diverse perspective in health. I came across the MSc in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation at the University of Oxford’s Nuffield Department of Medicine. It aligned with many of my interests, so I applied. I also needed a scholarship because, quite frankly, I couldn’t afford Oxford. It was a humbling and affirming process. I was awarded scholarships such as the Chevening Scholarship and two Oxford-based scholarships. I still feel fortunate to have received and chosen the Mastercard Foundation-Africa Oxford Initiative Scholarship, which fully funded my studies. I am deeply grateful for that opportunity. Now, I think it’s important to say that I was very excited about the academic programme. I wanted to understand healthcare systems better, learn new research methods and become more effective at designing and evaluating healthcare services. However, I was also very excited about everything else. I was going to be at Oxford! There were going to be people from different countries

item.title: Software issues have even reached Mercury as BepiColombo probe arrives in uncertain state
item.description: Humanity’s third-ever mission to Mercury has arrived, but a last-minute “software issue” has complicated matters. The BepiColombo mission is a joint effort by the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Reaching Mercury is not easy because its gravity is weak and its orbit is fast. The tiny planet’s proximity to the Sun further complicates matters, because our star’s gravity accelerates everything that falls towards it. BepiColombo’s journey has therefore seen it whiz past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times on a complicated path the two space agencies designed to slow it down sufficiently to be captured by mercurial gravity, while also keeping up with its rapid orbit. In 2024, the craft’s thrusters underperformed, leading the ESA and JAXA to re-plot the planned trajectory and reschedule its arrival at Mercury from mid-2025 to this past weekend. The ESA’s operations team sent the commands to insert BepiColombo into orbit on Friday. On Sunday the craft phoned home with news that it entered orbit. A little later, however, the ESA revealed “the thruster burn was shorter than planned following a software issue.” The spacecraft is safe, but the ESA says it is “working to understand what happened” and promised updates early this week. Readers may recall that a pair of NASA missions to Mars are also experiencing software glitches , which have in recent weeks become all-too-prevalent on Earth, too. Fingers crossed If all is well, BepiColombo will deploy two orbiters. The ESA’s craft is called the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), which the ESA says will map the planet, assess the composition of its surface and interior, measure its magnetic field, and even gather data that scientists hope will “test Einstein's theory of General Relativity to an unprecedented level of accuracy.” JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MIO) will also investigate the planet’s magnetic field, plasma, dust, and atmosphere. Both orbiters are extraordinary feats of engineering. As JAXA explains , MIO is solar-powered but the sunlight it will receive at Mercury is around ten times as powerful as on Earth. Mercury itself is also sufficiently hot that the orbiter needs protection from heat radiated from the planet’s surface. ESA’s MPO keeps itself cool with three to four insulating blankets comprised of layered titanium, aluminum, and a ceramic fabric called Nextel. The blankets alone weigh 94kg. The two space agencies expect to start science operations in April 2027 but haven’t yet said if the two orbiters are in peak condition. JAXA, sadly, last week revealed that its Hayabusa2 probe has deteriorated to the point at which it can no longer make its planned landing on asteroid 1998 KY26. JAXA scheduled that for the year 2031, but problems with the probe’s thrusters mean the agency will instead attempt a high-speed fly-by of asteroid 2015 BM510 in 2028. Hayabusa2 launched in 2014, so is rather older than BepiColombo. Humanity has visite

item.title: Techie turned his too-easy job interview into a trap
item.description: Returning to work after the weekend can feel like voluntarily walking into a trap. To help readers feel a little freer, The Register therefore uses Monday mornings to serve up a new installment of " Who, Me? " It's the column in which we share your stories of mistakes, misjudgments, and occasional misanthropy. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Marshall," who told us about a job interview he endured about 20 years ago. The interview included a practical component he described as "Here's a PC, we've broken a few things in it, get it going." Marshall quickly spotted some mundane faults, such as a loose PCI card and unplugged internal cables. He felt the test was too easy. "One of the things I always checked was whether the power supply 110/230 switch was set for the UK," he told The Register . Getting the PC running earned Marshall a job offer, but he couldn't resist suggesting a tougher test. "I said to my future manager: 'Would it be a good thing to set the power supply to the wrong voltage as part of the interview test?' He said that wasn't fair." Marshall stayed in the job for two years. A couple of months after he left, his former manager sent him a short email. "Ha-ha, very funny." Marshall asked another former colleague what might have prompted that email. "It turned out somebody – I don't know if it was an interview candidate – had blown a power supply by not checking the voltage it was set to." What a coincidence! Or maybe not? "It wasn't anything to do with me," Marshall insisted. "No idea who it was." Have you held colleagues to a higher standard than the boss expected? Or left a little trap for them to trip over? In either case, click here to send email to Who, Me? We appreciate the chance to share your stories, and do so with appropriate anonymization so that contributors never step into the jaws of trouble. ®

item.title: Laser Focus at the Top of the World
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Laser Focus at the Top of the… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search The Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory is located on the west coast of Spitsbergen, an island in Norway’s Svalbard archipelago, shown in this image acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on July 30, 2026. NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin More than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors. By measuring the time it took for the light to return, they demonstrated a new, more precise method for tracking satellites. Since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used. The technique now underpins many aspects of Earth observation, such as validating satellite orbits and mapping subtle changes to Earth’s surface. Pioneered at the Goddard Optical Research Facility—now the Goddard Geophysical and Astronomical Observatory —laser ranging is performed at more than 40 stations worldwide. In 2026, the next generation of SLR, developed by NASA scientists and tested at Goddard, began to come online. On October 12, a faster, even more precise SLR system officially debuted at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory in Svalbard, Norway, operated by the Norwegian Mapping Authority, a NASA partner. The observatory’s remote location in the Arctic archipelago is shown in this image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 in July 2026. It is the first NASA next-generation SLR system in operation and the northernmost SLR facility on Earth. While the systems developed decades ago have been “workhorses” of the global laser tracking network, their age and the growing number of satellites have necessitated updates, said Stephen Merkowitz, project manager for NASA’s Space Geodesy Project . “We wanted newer systems that could track more objects, and track them more accurately and precisely,” he said. The Space Geodesy Satellite Laser Ranging system fires at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory in Svalbard, Norway, against a backdrop of aurora borealis on October 7, 2026. NASA/Julie Horvath (KBR) Years of development, testing, and careful calibration produced the Space Geodesy Satellite Laser Ranging system now running at Ny-Ålesund. Among its features are lasers that can fire pulses thousands of times per second, up from tens of times per second, and sensors that can detect single photons, meaning that less light needs to be reflected back from a satellite. Along with determining the orbits of satellites, SLR is critical for es

item.title: Google claims last week’s critical VMware bug was under attack in September
item.description: Google’s Mandiant unit has claimed that the critical flaw VMware last week revealed in its vCenter product was under attack by a China-linked threat actor which knew of the bug in July and exploited it in September. VMware revealed several flaws on November 19. The big nasty is CVE-2026-123890, which allows unauthorized access to vCenter, the management console for hosts and guest VMs. According to seven researchers from Google’s threat intelligence group (formerly Mandiant), a crew it calls ARMORY CASTLE that it suspects of having links to the People’s Republic of China exploited CVE-2026-123890 by first compromising remote access appliances from BeyondTrust. Google’s analysis suggests the crew uses that toehold to establish access to other Linux appliances before moving deeper into victims’ networks. If the crew finds vCenter, it deploys a custom malware tool called “BONESAW” designed to slice into the VMware product. In the incident Google observed, BONESAW let attackers “forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user.” The gang put that access to work by conducting an inventory of the victim’s VMware setup, scooping up data describing the ESXi file system, attached disks, and mounted Virtual Machine File System volumes. ARMORY CASTLE also added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys, and “conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account.” Google also found evidence of BONESAW being used in July, on a server an unidentified entity had patched against CVE-2026-59309 – another authentication bypass vulnerability in vCenter. And BONESAW was just one of five tools Google thinks ARMORY CASTLE created as part of its plan to attack vCenter. It also made webshells named SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, a backdoor called BEARBONES, and a SAML utility called SAWSNAKE. “The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations,” Google’s researchers wrote. “It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets.” Few targets are as juicy as vCenter, because it can literally give attackers access to thousands of virtual machines and the hosts they run on. Google hasn't said how many attacks is saw on vCenter using BONESAW. The Register asked VMware if it was aware of the September attack, if it took any measures to defend its customers at the time, and to share a timeline for disclosure and remediation of CVE-2026-123890. A spokesperson responded by pointing to VMware’s Q&A document and stating “In today's threat environment, customers should assume any publicly disclosed critical vulnerability can and will be exploited by threat actors under the right conditions and should apply the recommended patches immediately.” VMware has tried to make that easier by adding non-disruptive patching to several of it

item.title: $1 of GPT-5.1 tokens finds new ways around China’s Great Firewall
item.description: Researchers have found new ways to evade China’s Great Firewall after spending just $1 worth of tokens. That result appeared last week in a paper titled “CircumVolve: Automated Discovery of Censorship Evasion Strategies Using Large Language Models” presented at the Conference on Computer and Communications Security run by the Association for Computing Machinery’s Special Interest Group on Security, Audit and Control. Penned by six researchers from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Colorado Boulder, and activist group the Great Firewall Report, the paper points out that finding holes in the Great Firewall is a laborious process – so just the kind of task worth handing to AI. The authors came up with a tool they call “CircumVolve” and describe as “a system for automated discovery of censorship circumvention strategies across the full network stack.” “CircumVolve combines LLM code generation with iterative feedback-driven evaluation to produce verifiable and deployable evasion techniques,” they wrote. “CircumVolve models different censorship techniques as discrete scenarios, each capturing the specific context, protocol constraints, and blocking mechanisms of real-world censors. Within each scenario, evasion strategies are represented as executable Python programs that implement packet and protocol manipulations — from rewriting TCP/IP header fields, to crafting DNS queries that exploit parser ambiguities, to modifying the internal structure of encrypted QUIC Initial packets — while maintaining protocol correctness within tolerable bounds or strategically violating it when beneficial.” The authors tested CircumVolve on simulated censorship tools used by China, Iran, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan, and on virtual private servers deployed on clouds in those countries. Those tests found the median API cost to the first successful evasion was less than $1 in token expenditure costs when using GPT-5.1. The authors acknowledge that operators of censorship infrastructure might be able to observe CircumVolve at work, but feel its relatively small payloads – 80 KB of outgoing and 150 KB of incoming traffic – and 25-45-second pauses between tests might see it fly under the radar. “CircumVolve represents a first step in leveraging LLMs to accelerate the censorship-circumvention lifecycle,” the authors wrote. “By automating the labor-intensive tasks of protocol analysis, implementation, and testing, AI-driven approaches make studying circumvention capabilities far more accessible to the comparatively under-resourced Internet freedom community [and] demonstrates how AI-assisted systems can narrow the resource gap between Internet freedom advocates and well-funded censoring states.” Lenovo finally cracks monster datacenter profits Ever since acquiring IBM’s x86 server business in 2014, Chinese hardware giant Lenovo has struggled to turn a profit from datacenter sales, even as it expanded its business into storage, networking, and selling to hypersc

item.title: As cars go digital, US consumers pay an extra $12 billion a year for repairs
item.description: The computerization of cars comes at a price to US consumers, according to the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), which says that software fees and other charges faced by mechanics push up garage costs. An investigation by the non-profit consumer group estimates that car repair costs for Americans have been inflated by $12 billion each year, as vehicles integrate more computerized functions. Its report, Closing Shop , is available online. To find a failed sensor, release an electronic parking brake, or perform diagnostics, a technician has to first connect a laptop or tablet to the vehicle. To so this, the repair shop has to have the right software tools, and that means paying the vehicle manufacturer subscription charges and other fees, in order to get the information they need to complete the job. If smaller independent repair shops can’t afford all the necessary software or subscriptions, they may be forced to steer customers to authorized dealerships for some fixes – about one in five jobs – and this allows the latter to charge more. PIRG claims that drivers pay for this through their insurance premiums, even if they never need to get their car fixed, because higher repair costs mean higher insurance claims. It says the price of auto insurance has risen three times as fast as the rest of the US economy since 2012. Even if mechanics do choose to pay for the software, they spend an estimated collective 83 million hours a year buying, downloading, logging in, and waiting. At typical repair rates, that adds up to $12 billion. A separate report from the PIRG Education Fund claims that a two-tiered repair model now exists, where independent sites conduct repairs with less information, less powerful diagnostic tools, and higher associated costs than the authorized dealerships. The advocacy group wants to see legislators take this issue in hand, and has a number of recommendations for them. One is to stop manufacturers from locking out independent mechanics from simple repair jobs like changing brake pads, and require them to support a standard protocol for authenticating independent diagnostic tools. Another is to give owners control over their vehicle’s data via a standardized platform for accessing telematics repair information, so that the owner can give access to an independent repair shop. Car firms can use the vehicle data to tell owners that a repair is needed and to take it to an approved repair shop, without even disclosing what the issue is. DIY repairers should be able to get everything they need to fix their own cars. Service information and basic diagnostic software should be free, and PIRG also wants a cap on the license fees manufacturers charge for their official software tools. “We’ve allowed car manufacturers to build a toll road between the mechanic and the repair,” says Nathan Proctor, leader of PIRG’s Right to Repair campaign and co-author on the report. “We have a plethora of tolls on the road – subscriptions you need for m

item.title: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
item.description: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land. The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access. With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses. Read full article Comments

item.title: Elizabeth Agboola: Your Next Flight From Nigeria Could Be Two Holidays in One. Here’s How
item.description: Have you ever spent six hours in an airport waiting for your connecting flight, watching the departure screens, browsing duty-free shops and wondering what the city outside looks like? Perhaps you were connecting through Istanbul, Doha, Dubai or Addis Ababa. You were technically in another country, but the closest you came to experiencing it was buying a souvenir at the airport. What if I told you that some airlines could help you turn that connection into an additional holiday, sometimes even providing accommodation? Having travelled to more than 70 countries, I have learnt that one of the smartest ways to travel is to pay attention to the journey, not just the destination. Many Nigerians book international tickets based on price, travel time and baggage allowance. These are important considerations, but there is another question worth asking: What else can this ticket give me? I am talking about stopovers, not the hurried two-hour connection where you are running between terminals, but an intentional break in your journey that allows you to experience another destination before continuing to the country you originally planned to visit. And with the right airline, itinerary and travel documents, that additional experience might cost less than you imagine. First, Understand What You Are Booking A layover is generally a connection between flights; a stopover is a longer, planned break in your journey. Airlines define these differently, and the distinction matters because some offer special hotel packages, sightseeing tours or complimentary accommodation to qualifying passengers. For example, imagine travelling from Lagos to London through Istanbul. Instead of spending a few hours at Istanbul Airport, you could investigate whether your ticket qualifies for a longer stopover, allowing you to explore Istanbul before continuing to London. You have now turned one international journey into an opportunity to experience two destinations outside Nigeria. The secret is to investigate the stopover before purchasing your ticket, rather than arriving at the airport and hoping the airline will allow you to stay longer. Turkish Airlines: Turn Istanbul Into Part of Your Holiday Turkish Airlines operates a Stopover in Istanbul programme for eligible international passengers connecting through Istanbul Airport. For visa purposes, Nigerians do not qualify, but with a valid Turkish visa you would be able to qualify for some of the perks. Qualifying travellers with connections of at least 20 hours and up to seven days may receive complimentary hotel accommodation. Under the standard programme, eligible Economy Class passengers can receive one night in a four-star hotel, while Business Class passengers may receive two nights in a five-star or boutique hotel. Imagine travelling from Abuja or Lagos through Istanbul to London, Paris or another European destination. item.title: Come for the science, stay for the big iron: Supercomputer admin on why he loves the job
item.description: Web hosting might seem like an unlikely on-ramp to supercomputer administration, but it set Mark O'Shea on his way to running some of Australia's most powerful machines. O'Shea is team leader for supercomputing operations and senior supercomputing systems administrator at Australia's Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre . Pawsey is home to Setonix, an HPE Cray EX supercomputer with more than 200,000 AMD EPYC CPU cores and hundreds of AMD Instinct MI250X accelerators. Its GPU partition ranks 87th in the November TOP500 and 37th in the Green500 , which measures computational performance per watt. "Working in web hosting wasn't much different to what I was doing a few years later with supercomputers," O'Shea tells The Register . "Datacenters are essentially several thousand computers, as are supercomputers. "So, we essentially had the same problems," he says, especially as regards cooling and power management. There's no single formal route into supercomputer administration in Australia, O'Shea says. He picked up the necessary skills over time. Andrew Underwood, Dell's chief technology officer for high-performance computing and artificial intelligence across the Asia-Pacific, Japan, and China, says that lack of formal training means some supercomputer admins start in academia. He's observed that many HPC admins emerge from the sciences, catching the computing bug during their studies. A biologist working with a massive genomics database, for example, might discover a taste for running the systems behind it. "The biologist might decide they want to be someone working in IT helping other biologists transform their industry," Underwood says . "One of the things I really admire about people who work in the supercomputing field is they take it so seriously," Underwood adds. "It's almost a passion, a hobby, more so than it is a job." "They want to play that real supporting and foundational role of assisting and engaging with scientists to help them use the technology to solve the problems the world faces." O'Shea agrees, noting that many people who get into supercomputer admin are PhD graduates who stick around their universities after they graduate. Some of them gravitate toward running the departmental computers and then wind up in supercomputing. "There are many roles around universities allowing people to be introduced to [supercomputer administration] while still doing enterprise-style or more departmental admin for researchers and system administration," O'Shea says. Regardless of how a supercomputer admin gets their gig, both O'Shea and Underwood say the supersysadmin community is tight knit – which may not always be a good thing. "As an industry in supercomputing, we need to be open to people from diverse backgrounds," Underwood says, "and we need to build these frameworks like the Student Cluster Competition, conferences like eResearch and the SC Conference, where students can get educated and systems admins get exposed to continual training." item.title: AWS got hit by an outage too. Here's why you didn't hear about it
item.description: My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?" It's a great question! They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn g ot salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted. If you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike. AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds. But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?" Easy: it did. Everything breaks, all the time, including the narrative AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are currently smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed. But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most important region, us-east-1. At 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud ). The all-clear showed up at 6:53 AM. Every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS said in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. I do think it's patently unreasonable to blame them for this specific problem; "acts of war" are kinda hard to predict from the corporate planning meeting. A few things combined to help AWS out on November 15. First, it was pre-dawn Pacific time on Sunday. Most of us slept through it; my kids aren't even up that early. Further, the services that were most impacted (IAM Identity Center) were for engineers signing in to AWS accounts, not consumers staring at an app that stopped working. Plus, the competition sucked all the oxygen out of the room: a day-plus Microsoft 365 364 outage and a four-hour nationwide air traffic ground stop had done

item.title: ChatGPT shrunk down to run on a Super Nintendo
item.description: If you’ve ever wondered how small an instance of ChatGPT could get, wonder no longer. Someone has actually rigged up a tiny version of the chatbot to run on a Super Nintendo cartridge. Tech journalist and retro tech enthusiast Benj Edwards is responsible for ChatGPT for SNES . He's published it online running in an emulator, complete with SNES-era music and sound effects, and for download as an SNES ROM, too. It’s not a big model, mind you, and performance is thus pretty limited: According to the website, it’s a 2.2 million-parameter offshoot of OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-120b, which was used to develop its training conversations – so in that sense it truly is a ChatGPT that runs on an SNES cartridge. Edwards described it to The Register as a distilled version of the aforementioned open-weight model. There are two options built into ChatGPT for SNES: One that’s purely the model, with every word generated coming right from its tiny little silicon brain, and another that includes a fact book culled from the opening sentences of around 150,000 simple English Wikipedia articles. If you opt to run both versions and ask it the same questions, you’ll notice a massive difference. Given some of the other responses we got while testing, there’s really no good reason to run the base model – memory isn’t really an issue given the basic build is about 4MB and the factbook build is just 19MB. Edwards admits that it’s not the most helpful AI model, either – this is just an experiment after all. “It is not a useful assistant: the model is millions of times smaller than the models behind ChatGPT, knows about 8,000 words, and often gets things wrong, sometimes confidently,” Edwards noted in his writeup. In that sense, it really is vintage AI on vintage hardware. “The fact book can carry mistakes too.” If you have an SNES lying around (lucky you), you can download the ROM from this link. If you want to get it running on an SNES you’ll need a cartridge that allows running of custom ROMs, and that supports Nintendo’s Super FX graphics coprocessor. Cartridges like the FXPak Pro and SD2SNES support it. The factbook version also requires support for the aftermarket Media Streaming Unit 1 (MSU-1), which adds CD-ROM like features to the SNES. MSU-1 is available in both of the flash carts mentioned above. If you have some real hardware skills, however, you could technically make your own ChatGPT cartridge. “The ‘pure’ version, which generates all responses from the AI language model, could run from a real custom SNES cart,” Edwards told us – it doesn’t even actually need the Super FX chip. “I do have a version of ChatGPT for SNES that can run without the Super FX chip, but without the extra processing power the answers are not as good.” That said, Edwards believes its absolutely crazy and nonsensical answers are part of the fun. “ChatGPT for SNES can definitely make mistakes too, but it's almost cute when it does it because of its limited knowledge and its playful interface,” Edward

item.title: NASA Mars rover and orbiter suffer glitches
item.description: It's been a bad few weeks for technology on and off the planet, as NASA reported problems with its Perseverance Mars rover and Odyssey orbiter this week. For Perseverance, the problem seems to be a relatively straightforward communications issue that has paused science operations because of low data rates. The Odyssey orbiter, however, is facing an issue that could end the mission. The 2001 Mars Odyssey reached orbit around Mars in October 2001 to search for evidence of water and ice on the surface. The mission was supposed to last two and a half years, but the spacecraft's operations have been extended for a quarter of a century. In that time, it has had its fair share of ups and downs, including the failure of one of its four reaction wheels in 2013. Three reaction wheels are needed to orient the spacecraft; otherwise, it must fall back to its hydrazine thrusters. Earlier in November, between the 4th and 6th, Odyssey dropped into safe mode, which engineers determined was caused by one of the remaining reaction wheels stopping spinning. Science data stopped flowing as the team worked to recover the component; the good news was that the wheel moved when commanded. The bad news is that if the thrusters need to be used, only a few months of fuel remain. More bad news is that the spacecraft is part of NASA's Mars Relay Network, and was responsible for sending back the first post-landing images from the Phoenix lander and the Spirit, Opportunity, and Curiosity rovers. Its loss (should it come to that) would therefore be keenly felt. In the event the orbiter is indeed approaching the end of the road, the European Space Agency's Mars Express (MEX) and Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) could pick up some of the load although, as a former ESA insider put it: "MEX is a science mission that can do relay where TGO is a relay mission that also does science." According to NASA, TGO already sends the most relay data from Mars to Earth. The challenge facing the Perseverance trundlebot is one of communication. On October 30, the rover's main computer detected problems with the primary radio (a series of "heartbeats" from the device did not arrive as expected) and automatically switched to a redundant backup, placing itself in a protective safe mode. So far, so expected. Engineers brought the rover back from safe mode, analyzed the data, and made an unpleasant discovery. The backup radio was not performing as it should – it was operating at approximately half of its expected power output. Both radios were therefore deemed inoperable – at least until the team has got to the bottom of the issues – and the rover has used X-band communications over its high-gain antenna to talk to Earth ever since. The problem here is that the connection provides a significantly lower data rate, meaning science and instrument operations are on hold. Engineers are working first to return the backup radio to operational status, then to address the primary. ®

item.title: Amazon's split personality: AWS embraces bot commerce while main site enforces bans
item.description: Amazon is of two minds when it comes to automated purchasing. The ecommerce giant has been busy banning AI shopping agents from accessing its website. Meanwhile, AWS Marketplace has opened its door to bot-based buying. "Buying software and data through AWS Marketplace just got easier, for you and for the AI agents working alongside you," said Mya Papolu, product marketing manager for AWS Marketplace and Partner Services at Amazon Web Services, in a blog post this week. "For re:Invent 2026, we’re launching capabilities designed to reduce friction across the buying journey." For a company that has blocked bots from Google, Meta, and OpenAI, and sued Perplexity to keep its AI-encumbered Comet browser away, the openness of AWS Marketplace to agentic commerce invites questions. We asked Amazon to explain but we've not heard back. AWS Marketplace is allowing AI agents to scour its site and buy some cloud software products using the x402 agentic payment protocol , which is supported by Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments. Introduced by Coinbase and Cloudflare , x402 got handed over to the Linux Foundation earlier this year, and now has support from a variety of tech platforms, including AWS, Google, Stripe, and various blockchain networks. About a week ago, Brave Software announced support for x402 payments through its search API. AWS requires sellers to register with AWS Marketplace and to integrate the AWS Marketplace x402 SDK to enable agentic product purchases. Transactions settle in USD through AWS billing so existing spending controls can be applied. And now, customers in the US can buy some AWS Marketplace software without an AWS account; instead they're asked to provide an email or social media login, and a credit card. While AWS Marketplace today lists mainly familiar software categories (Business Applications, Data & Analytics, DevOps, Infrastructure Software, and so on), AWS has a broader product inventory in mind. Beyond software and APIs, the biz sees a future in selling content and data. Papolu announced that AWS is now selling " data as a service ." "Data providers can list their offerings in AWS Marketplace, making commercial data accessible to both human teams and the agents working alongside them via the AWS Marketplace website, APIs, and MCP server," she said. This includes services like Moody's Credit MCP server for financial research; Reuters Geopolitical News for AI-structured reporting; US Building Permits, Contractors & Residents Data from Shovels; and US-EN Multi-Speaker Conversational Acoustic Corpus from Uber AI Solutions. In canned remarks provided to AWS, Nandhan Puppala, general manager at Uber AI Solutions, said that data quality and readiness can help advance AI products. Agent mode for AWS Marketplace has been available for about a year as a way to query the market via prompt. That's being expanded to allow deeper queries about seller security and project requirements. Science fiction writer William Gibson's oft-cited line

item.title: PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here
item.description: On Thursday, PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month. For those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server. Users of every PHP-based application, including WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony, had to scramble to update their PHP instances. The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation , responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP ( 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep. In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the new version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings. Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults. Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.” No cookies for impostors In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline . Code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit. For Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote. Furthermore, PHP will now, by default, add the HttpOnly flag to its session Set-Cookie header, blocking client-side JavaScript from reading the session ID, which could otherwise be stolen to masquerade as the user. Believe it or not, any script on the page could read it before. Finally, the server will withhold session cookies on cross-site POST requests, as well as for subrequests and iframes. “Without it, a forged form or link on an attacker-controlled site can trigger authenticated requests using the victim’s session,” Sowa wrote. Going forward, cookies will only be sent on same-site requests and top-level GET navigations, such as clicking a normal link. Collectively, these changes should thwart session hijacking and cross-site request forgeries. They won’t stop remote code execution hacks, though they will make it a lot more difficult for

item.title: Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers
item.description: Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses. On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information. Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand. Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers. “We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register . “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.” Mastercard previously said that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program. According to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker said. It’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker. Plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text, and CRM ID format, Seker said, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26. “This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he said. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.” Customer data has left the building The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published. All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security company Sentra. item.title: Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy
item.description: Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns. Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal President Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private. "Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post . "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private. Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text. Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents. Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS." Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately. With macOS 27.3 , currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs.
